summary: Describes DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV), a way to publish DNSSEC trust anchors outside the normal DNS delegation chain. It helped resolvers validate zones whose parents were unsigned or did not publish DS records. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: DNSSEC works like a chain of signatures. DLV was a side table to look up when the chain had a gap. It is now historic and no longer used.

subtitle: A side table in the DNS that let resolvers find DNSSEC trust anchors for zones whose parents were not signed.

tldr.problem: With the DNS root and many top-level domains unsigned, a validating resolver had to keep a large set of preconfigured trust anchors to validate signed zones.
tldr.mechanism: DLV domains publish DLV records, which a validator treats like DS records, for zones that are not their own children. The validator trusts them after validating the DLV domain from a single trust anchor.
tldr.outcome: Operators could outsource trust anchor management. The RFC is Informational and is now marked Historic.

today: RFC 5074 is marked Historic, and no replacement RFC is named in its metadata. The record type it uses is defined in RFC 4431.

sections.title: Why Lookaside Validation
sections.content:
DNSSEC authenticates DNS data by building public-key signature chains along the delegation chain, starting from a trust anchor. When the RFC was written, the DNS root and many key top-level domains were unsigned. The only way for a validating resolver to validate the many signed zones was to keep a sizable collection of preconfigured trust anchors, which is a significant management challenge.

DLV publishes trust anchors in the DNS outside the normal delegation chain. It lets an organization configure many validators easily, or outsource trust anchor management.
sections.eli5: If the top of the family tree is missing, you would have to remember every family on its own. DLV is a shared notebook that someone else keeps up to date.

sections.title: DLV Domains
sections.content:
A validator can expect a zone to be secure if it has a preconfigured trust anchor for the zone, or a validated DS record in the parent zone. DLV adds a third way: a validated entry in a DLV domain, which in turn needs a trust anchor for that DLV domain. A missing DLV RRset does not mean a zone is insecure. If the validator has another reason to expect signatures, it should still try to validate.

Each DLV domain makes statements about descendants of one target zone. The name for a zone is built by replacing the target zone name with the DLV domain name. If trustbroker.example.com targets org, DLV records for example.org live at example.trustbroker.example.com. If bar.example.com targets the root, they live at example.org.bar.example.com.

A DLV domain needs little besides DLV records, the DNSSEC records that validate them, and apex NS and SOA records. It SHOULD NOT use minimally-covering NSEC records or NSEC3, so that aggressive negative caching works well.
sections.eli5: The notebook is organized by the same names as the real addresses, just with the notebook owner's name added on the end.

sections.title: How a Validator Uses DLV
sections.content:
A validator SHOULD first try validation with any ordinary trust anchors. If that gives Secure, DLV is not needed. Otherwise, with a trust anchor for a DLV domain, it SHOULD validate all responses at and below that domain's target.

It searches for the closest enclosing DLV RRset. It starts at the query name and removes the leading label each time a validated NSEC proves there is no DLV RRset, until it finds one or proves none exists. For a query about sub.example.org, a record at sub.example.trustbroker.example.com is used before the shorter ones.

The DLV RRset or the proof of non-existence MUST be validated with the normal procedures in Section 5 of RFC 4035. A Bogus or Insecure DLV result must not be used, and the original response SHOULD get the same result. A Secure DLV RRset is then treated as a DS RRset. Validators SHOULD NOT use DLV to validate data from another DLV domain.
sections.eli5: Look for the exact page first. If it is not there, flip back to a more general page, until you find one or know there is none.

sections.title: Caching and Overlap
sections.content:
To reduce load on DLV servers, validators SHOULD implement aggressive negative caching. Besides matching exact cached negative answers, a validator checks whether any cached and validated NSEC record denies the sought name, and does not query for any name that NSEC covers. Unless the CD bit was set, it can synthesize a negative answer from that NSEC.

In an optimization, authoritative servers SHOULD put all DLV RRsets applicable to the query name and its ancestors in the Additional section, along with NSEC records proving no others exist. Validators MAY cache and use that data if it validates.

Several DLV domains may overlap, for example two targeting org, or one targeting the root and one org. Precedence is left to the implementation and SHOULD be a configuration option. A simple default is to prefer the most specific DLV domain.
sections.eli5: If you already know a whole range of names is not in the notebook, you do not need to look each one up again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Validators MUST NOT use a DLV record unless it has been successfully authenticated. Aggressive negative caching makes it more important to check incoming NSEC records. The next name field MUST be within the zone that signed the NSEC. Otherwise an "overreaching" NSEC could spoof away names in ancestor zones, even up to the root.

Validators MUST NOT treat the mere presence of an RRSIG or apex DNSKEY RRset as a trigger for validation, or an attacker could strip them in a downgrade attack. As for DS records, the key tag helps select a DNSKEY but does not uniquely identify one, so using it alone might select the wrong key.

The IANA section notes that DLV uses the DLV resource record type 32769, assigned earlier in RFC 4431.
sections.eli5: Only believe a notebook entry if it is properly signed, and never skip checking just because the signatures seem to be missing.
